messages.author: 14f111fb9c031270
messages.subject: TPB - Difference between Factor Analysis + regresion vs SEM
parts:
Hi there,
Jonathan here.. doing a phd an struggling a bit, so before hand thanks for reading this message in a bottle.
I'm pretty new to lavaan and SEM in general. Can someone explain me the difference between these approaches, if you want i can provide the results, but since they are quite extensive, i could attach on demand.
I'm working with the Theory of Planned Behavior, lets say
- a1,a2,a3,a4 are for construct A
- s1,s2,s3,s4 are for construct S
- p1,p2,p3,p4 are for construct P
Then my model has two regressions:
Int ~A + S + P
Beh ~ P + Int

So far, so good... i can run this and perform some evaluations,
but then i was wondering using pca to reduce my a1,a2,...s1....p4, and extract 3 factors.
Lets call these, A_x, S_x and P_X
Then I could run a sem
Int ~A_x + S _x + P _x
Beh ~ P _x + Int

--> for some reason this model adjust better than the one before.

Finally, i run 2 regressions (with low explanatory power 20%-40%)
Int ~A_x + S _x + P _x
Beh ~ P _x + Int

Besides validation of TPB, I'm interested on extracting coefficients so that i can use them in a simulation (agent-based model) to recreate the behavior.

Please if someone has been working with this issues or has faced similar questions, any pointer will be very very useful!

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: TPB - Difference between Factor Analysis + regresion vs SEM
parts:
Jonathan--
     This is a very extensive and fundamental topic. If you really want to understand the differences between PCA and common factor analysis (and you don't mind some math), I might recommend Stanley Mulaik's (2010) Foundations of Factor Analysis, where Ch. 9 covers PCA and related composite-based methods.
     To try to be brief...the difference in results depends partly on:
whether or not the variances of the observed variables are generally the same or are different--PCA finds the largest hunk of variance across the set of observed variables, and that could be mostly just one of the original variables, if its variance is much larger than the rest; 
 the covariance structure of the data--if a correlated factor model is correct for the data, then a PCA will tend to underestimate relations between composites relative to factors, because the factor model sets aside variance that is unique to the observed variables, while the PCA does not, necessarily;
whether the factor model loadings are strong or weak--if they are weak enough, then you could get something radically different from PCA;
     I don't know what you mean by "adjusts better." Your second analysis produces a model which is more saturated / has fewer degrees of freedom, so it may well seem to better fit the data--but maybe only because it faces a less severe test.
     https://www.amazon.com/Foundations-Analysis-Statistics-Behavioral-Sciences-ebook/dp/B005H6YSNC/ref=sr_1_fkmr2_1?crid=245C2LUAYL0B6&keywords=mulaik+fundamentals+of+factor+analysis&qid=1685586546&sprefix=mulaik+fundamentals+of+factor+analysis%2Caps%2C94&sr=8-1-fkmr2

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: TPB - Difference between Factor Analysis + regresion vs SEM
parts:
Hello Jonathan,

If you first extract 'scores' for the latent variables (either using PCA
or any other method), and then plug them in a regression, you are using
a 'structural-after-measurement' (SAM) approach (in the case of PCA
without correcting for measurement error).

You may want to have a look at this paper:

https://psycnet.apa.org/doiLanding?doi=10.1037%2Fmet0000503

In principle, when extracting latent 'scores', you should take the
measurement error into account (to avoid bias in the regression
coefficients). But if your sample size is rather small (say <200), this
is not necessarily the best approach, as we observed in simulation
studies that 'uncorrected' methods often result in much lower
mean-squared-error (MSE) values, see for example:

https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/00131644221105505

My apologies for referring only to my own work, but this happens to be
one of the research lines in our lab.

Yves.
